newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU health chief attacks tobacco subsidies.
newsitem.headline: EU health chief attacks tobacco subsidies.

text.p: European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn plans to attack the European Union's tobacco subsidies on Wednesday, arguing that they compromise its anti-smoking drive and give its critics ammunition.

Flynn, as part of his long-running battle to cut tobacco-related deaths in the EU, will urge his colleagues to phase out production subsidies in an effort to forge a coherent policy, EU officials said.

"Of perhaps greatest concern is the fact that the existing policy on tobacco is used to attack and discredit Commission policy more generally," he argues in a paper that has been circulated to his colleagues.

However, Flynn is opposed by Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, who argues that EU member states would never agree to such a radical proposal and that ending subsidies would not curb smoking since the vast majority of EU tobacco is imported.
"If we make a very radical proposal, we end up with the status quo because it won't go anywhere," a Commission agriculture source said, noting that eight EU countries produce tobacco.
Flynn's paper, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, will be discussed during an orientation debate by the Commission on Wednesday over the future of EU subsidies to tobacco farmers.

The debate was planned to guide the Commission as it draws up two policy papers, a report on the common organisation of the tobacco market to be drafted by Fischler and a communication on new measures to cut tobacco consumption to be drafted by Flynn.
Flynn complained that the EU paid almost 993 million Ecus to support tobacco production in 1995, while devoting only 15 million Ecus annually to discourage smoking.

The EU produces only 5.4 percent of the world's tobacco, but Commission agriculture sources said cutting off tobacco subsidies would put 135,000 farmers, in addition to many seasonal workers, out of work. EU farmers grow tobacco on small plots averaging one hectare that cannot be easily devoted to other crops, they said.
Italy is the EU's biggest tobacco producer, followed by Greece, with farms also found in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Portugal and Spain.
Fischler proposes "deepening" reforms that were introduced in 1992, which ended export refunds and public purchases of tobacco and introduced quotas and quality controls.

Flynn's spending comparisons are unfair because they do not take into account national spending on public health programmes, a Commission agriculture source said. The EU has sole jurisdiction over tobacco subsidies, he added.
Flynn's paper concedes that the EU would have to provide "large-scale" financial assistance to help the tobacco sector adjust if it abolished subsidies.
He complained that the quality of EU tobacco is on average so low that its commercial value is only one fifth of the subsidies that are used to grow it.
